'The agency says the attendant can start Monday, eight to five,' said Sabina.
'Trained? First aid and all?'
'Yes. And they'll follow whatever schedule we give. Breakfast at eight, tablets after, physio at eleven, lunch at one.'
'And Dr Rao on Thursdays.' Shalini typed as they talked. 'I'm putting it all on the shared calendar. Green for meals, blue for the doctor, red for anything unusual.'
'Will Abba mind a stranger in the house?'
'He'll grumble for a week. Then he'll enjoy having someone to play chess with.'
'And if there's a problem?'
'Then the red entry shows up on both our phones, and one of us calls the agency, not each other in a panic.'
Three weeks later Sabina texted in the middle of a meeting: 'No calls from home today.'
'That's what we paid for,' Shalini wrote back.

qa.a: Green for meals, blue for the doctor, and red for anything unusual.

qa.q: What is Sabina worried about with the new attendant?
qa.a: Sabina is worried that Abba will mind having a stranger in the house.

qa.q: What could help Abba settle in with the attendant?
qa.a: Abba could help shape the routine and be introduced to the attendant with family present on the first day, and the chess games could give them something to share.

qa.q: How might Abba see the new arrangement?
qa.a: Abba may feel a little intruded upon at first, but could also feel relieved to have steady company and less worry about being a burden.

grounding: Shalini and Sabina hire a trained daytime attendant, set a fixed schedule and use a shared calendar to reduce work-hour emergencies.

subtopic: Caring for ageing parents while working
subtype: Approach: arranging paid help and a routine [Action]
passage:
For most of last year, my phone would ring during office meetings and my heart would sink. Appa had forgotten his lunch again, or missed his doctor's appointment, or Amma couldn't lift him from the chair alone.
My brother Omkar and I finally sat down in January and admitted we couldn't keep rushing home from two different offices.
We hired a trained attendant through an agency, Mr. Pillai, who comes from nine to six on weekdays. Then we fixed a schedule and stuck it on the kitchen wall: breakfast at eight-thirty, medicines after each meal, lunch at one, a short walk at five. Doctor visits always on the first Monday, when Omkar takes a half day.
We also made a shared calendar on our phones, so all three of us, Omkar, Amma and I, can see what's happening.
Since February, my phone has rung during work exactly twice.
— Santosh

qa.q: What hours does Mr. Pillai work?
qa.a: From nine to six on weekdays.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel when the phone rang during meetings last year?
qa.a: Santosh felt anxious and dreaded each call, with a sinking heart.

qa.q: What else could Santosh and Omkar prepare for days Mr. Pillai is unwell?
qa.a: They could agree a backup, such as the agency sending a replacement, and keep emergency contacts on the shared calendar.

qa.q: How might Amma experience the new routine?
qa.a: Amma no longer has to lift Appa alone or chase him about lunch, so she likely feels less strained and more supported.

grounding: It shows a family hiring a trained daytime attendant, fixing a schedule for meals and doctor visits and using a shared calendar to reduce emergencies during work hours.

Home-care coordinator's note — Sabina's family, Mysore Road. Written by Rafiq.

When I first met Sabina in April, she had taken leave four times in one month. Her mother, who lives with her, has Parkinson's, and Sabina and her husband both work in the city.
Together we set up three things. First, a trained attendant from our agency, eight to five on weekdays. Second, a fixed routine we wrote together and pinned on the fridge: medicines at set times, meals at the same hours, a short exercise session after breakfast, doctor visits on the second Wednesday of each month. Third, a shared phone calendar that Sabina, her husband, the attendant and I can all see.
At our review in July, Sabina said she'd had only one work call about her mother in six weeks. "And that was just a question about lunch," she laughed.
My next step: a three-monthly review, since needs can change.

qa.q: On which Wednesday are the doctor visits?
qa.a: The second Wednesday of each month.

qa.q: How did Sabina seem to feel at the July review?
qa.a: Sabina seemed relieved and more relaxed, laughing that the only call had been a question about lunch.

qa.q: What else could Sabina's family add to the arrangement?
qa.a: They could list backup contacts and a nearby hospital in the shared calendar, in case of an emergency when the attendant is off.

qa.q: How might Sabina's mother experience the fixed routine?
qa.a: Her mother likely feels more settled and safe, with the same people, times and meals each day instead of rushed arrangements.

grounding: It shows, through a coordinator's note, a family hiring a daytime attendant, setting a fixed schedule for meals and doctor visits and using a shared calendar.
